phase1.explanation:
Sometimes order doesn't matter and duplicates are actively wrong — a guest list, a set of tags, a list of student IDs you've already processed. That's what [[term:Set]] is for: [[key:membership is the entire point, and every element appears at most once]], no matter how many times you try to add it again.

[[term:HashSet]] is the default choice — backed by a hash table, so add(), contains(), and remove() are all O(1) average case. The trade-off is right there in the name: no guaranteed order. Print a HashSet twice in the same run and you'll usually get the same order, but that's an implementation detail, not a promise — [[warn:never write code that depends on HashSet's iteration order]].

[[term:TreeSet]] trades that speed for structure — it keeps elements in sorted order at all times, backed by a red-black tree, which pushes add()/contains()/remove() to O(log n). In exchange you get first(), last(), and neighbor-lookups like lower() and higher() for free — none of which HashSet can offer, because HashSet has no sense of "before" or "after" at all.

One catch that trips people up with [[term:custom objects]]: a HashSet only knows two Person objects are "the same" if equals() and hashCode() say so. Without overriding both, every new Person() looks unique to the set — even if the name and age are identical — because the default equals() just compares memory addresses. [[fun:this is exactly why every class you write that might end up in a Set or as a Map key needs its own equals()/hashCode() pair]].

mcq.question:
You need to store a growing list of usernames, guarantee no duplicates, and you'll frequently need them printed alphabetically for a report. Which is the single best fit?

A) ArrayList, sorting manually before each report
B) HashSet — fastest add/contains, order doesn't matter here anyway
C) TreeSet — no duplicates AND always sorted, no manual sort step needed
D) LinkedList, since it preserves insertion order

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a program that:
1. Creates an ArrayList<Integer> with numbers: [1, 2, 3, 2, 4, 3, 5, 1, 6]
2. Creates a HashSet<Integer> from the list (removing duplicates)
3. Prints the HashSet
4. Creates a TreeSet<Integer> from the same list
5. Prints the TreeSet (should be sorted)
6. Prints the size of both sets
7. Checks if both sets contain the number 4

phase5.trivia: HashSet is actually built on top of HashMap internally — every element you add becomes a key in a hidden HashMap, mapped to a shared dummy placeholder value. That's why HashSet and HashMap share the same O(1) average-case performance and the same equals()/hashCode() requirement.
